vercel-deploy.md:
## Why it exists
Deploying used to mean servers, SSH and manual steps. **Vercel** connects to your Git repository and turns every push into a deployment: a build, a global CDN and on-demand compute, with no servers to manage. It is built by the team behind Next.js but hosts many frameworks.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
1. Import a Git repository as a **project**. Vercel detects the framework and sets the build commands.
2. Every push to a non-production branch creates a **preview deployment** with its own URL.
3. Merging to the production branch creates a **production deployment** served on your domains.
4. Each deployment is immutable. **Rollback** means pointing your domain at an earlier deployment, which is near-instant.

## Environment variables
| Environment | Used for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Production | The live site | Real database and API keys |
| Preview | Every branch and pull request | Point at staging services, never production data |
| Development | `vercel dev` and `vercel env pull` | Pulled into a local .env.local file |
```bash
vercel link                    # connect this folder to a project
vercel env pull .env.local     # download development variables
vercel deploy                  # create a preview deployment
vercel deploy --prod           # create a production deployment
```
Changing a variable does not affect existing deployments. Redeploy to apply it.

## In real products
- Use preview URLs for design review and QA, and run end-to-end tests against them in CI.
- Set the project **Root Directory** for monorepos, and use ignored build steps to skip apps a commit did not touch.
- Add domains in project settings and point DNS at Vercel. TLS certificates are issued automatically.
- Turn on **Deployment Protection** so previews are not public.

> [!security] In Next.js, variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are inlined into the browser bundle. Never put a secret key behind that prefix.
> [!pitfall] Pointing Preview deployments at the production database means every pull request can modify real data. Use a staging database or branching.
> [!tip] Supabase and Neon offer per-branch databases, which pair well with per-pull-request preview deployments.
q: Why does changing an environment variable not fix a live site immediately?
Each deployment is immutable and has its variables baked in at build or start; you must redeploy.
What is dangerous about a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable?
Its value is embedded in the JavaScript sent to every visitor, so it must never hold a secret.

vercel-functions.md:
## Why it exists
Your Next.js API routes and Server Components need somewhere to run. On Vercel that is **Vercel Functions**: code that runs on demand, scales automatically and needs no servers. Its execution model is called **Fluid compute**.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
Classic serverless gave every request its own instance, which wasted time whenever the function waited on a database or an API. **Fluid compute** reuses instances and lets one instance handle several requests concurrently (Node.js and Python runtimes). That cuts cold starts and cost, and billing focuses on active CPU time rather than time spent waiting. It is the default for new projects.

## Worked example
```ts
// app/api/report/route.ts
export const maxDuration = 60        // seconds this function may run

export async function GET() {
  const data = await fetchFromDb()   // I/O wait is cheap under Fluid compute
  return Response.json(data)
}
```

## Scheduled work with cron
```json
{
  "crons": [{ "path": "/api/cron/cleanup", "schedule": "0 3 * * *" }]
}
```
```ts
// app/api/cron/cleanup/route.ts
export async function GET(req: Request) {
  if (req.headers.get('authorization') !== `Bearer ${process.env.CRON_SECRET}`) {
    return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 })
  }
  await cleanup()
  return Response.json({ ok: true })
}
```
Vercel calls the path on the schedule and sends your `CRON_SECRET` as a bearer token, so strangers cannot trigger the endpoint.

## Limits and runtimes
| Topic | Current guidance |
|---|---|
| Runtimes | Node.js (default), Python, Bun and Rust; the older Edge runtime is not recommended for most new code |
| Default duration | 300 seconds; the maximum depends on plan (Hobby 300 seconds, Pro up to 800 seconds, with longer options in beta) |
| Concurrency | Scales automatically to very high limits |
| WebSockets | Supported on Fluid compute |
| Data | Blob storage for files; databases such as Neon, Supabase and Upstash come through the Marketplace |

Limits change with plans and releases, so confirm the numbers on the Vercel limits page before depending on them.

## In real products
- Webhooks (Stripe, GitHub) as route handlers, with signature verification.
- Streaming AI responses with the AI SDK, using longer durations.
- Nightly jobs and cache warmers with cron.
- Long or retry-heavy work goes to a queue (Vercel Queues or an external one), not to a single function.

> [!pitfall] Because one instance can serve several requests at once, module-level variables are shared between them. Never store per-request or per-user data in globals.
> [!pitfall] Vercel has moved databases to Marketplace integrations (Neon, Upstash, Supabase), which also provision environment variables. Check the current storage docs before planning around a native database product.
> [!cost] Streaming and long durations keep functions running. Set maxDuration deliberately and watch usage in the dashboard.
q: What problem does Fluid compute solve compared with one instance per request?
Instances sit idle while waiting on I/O; Fluid compute reuses an instance for other concurrent requests, reducing cold starts and cost.
Why is a module-level variable dangerous in a Vercel Function?
Concurrent requests share the same instance and module state, so per-request data can leak between users.
